lessons.title: Lab: Maximum depth of a binary tree

story.title: Maximum depth of a binary tree

scenes.text: A UI framework measures nesting depth of a component tree.
Interviewer: “Works? Good. Now what's the complexity — and can you beat brute force?”

steps.title: Problem
steps.body: One line: level-order values with 'null' for gaps. Print the maximum depth.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.body:
Recursion: 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right))

Post-order DFS; empty tree has depth 0.

steps.title: Walk-through
steps.body:
Input:
3 9 20 null null 15 7

Output: **3**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Counting edges instead of nodes.

steps.title: Complexity
steps.body: Time **O(n)**, extra space **O(h)**. Say both out loud in an interview, then mention the brute force you rejected.

activity.prompt: One line: level-order values with 'null' for gaps. Print the maximum depth.

quiz.q: Time complexity of the efficient solution to “Maximum depth of a binary tree”?
quiz.why: Post-order DFS; empty tree has depth 0. → O(n) time, O(h) extra space.

quiz.q:
“Maximum depth of a binary tree”: for the input below, what should the program print?
3 9 20 null null 15 7
quiz.why: Trace it: the expected output is 3.

quiz.q: Which idea solves “Maximum depth of a binary tree” efficiently?
options: In-order traversal yields sorted order; stop at k
Pre-order with null markers is unambiguous
quiz.why: Post-order DFS; empty tree has depth 0.

scenes.text: A build system must decide whether module dependencies can be ordered.
Interviewer: “Works? Good. Now what's the complexity — and can you beat brute force?”

steps.title: Problem
steps.body: Line 1: n m. Next m lines: a b meaning a depends on b. Print true if all n modules can be built.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.body:
Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly remove in-degree-0 nodes

If all nodes get removed there is no cycle.

steps.title: Walk-through
steps.body:
Input:
2 1
1 0

Output: **true**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Forgetting isolated nodes.

steps.title: Complexity
steps.body: Time **O(V+E)**, extra space **O(V+E)**. Say both out loud in an interview, then mention the brute force you rejected.

activity.prompt: Line 1: n m. Next m lines: a b meaning a depends on b. Print true if all n modules can be built.
activity.starter:
from collections import deque
n, m = map(int, input().split())
E = [tuple(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(m)]
# your code here
activity.solution:
from collections import deque
n, m = map(int, input().split())
E = [tuple(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(m)]
adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]; indeg = [0] * n
for a, b in E: adj[b].append(a); indeg[a] += 1
q = deque(i for i in range(n) if indeg[i] == 0); seen = 0
while q:
    u = q.popleft(); seen += 1
    for v in adj[u]:
        indeg[v] -= 1
        if indeg[v] == 0: q.append(v)
print('true' if seen == n else 'false')

quiz.why: If all nodes get removed there is no cycle. → O(V+E) time, O(V+E) extra space.

1 0
quiz.why: Trace it: the expected output is true.

quiz.q: Which idea solves “Course schedule (cycle detection)” efficiently?
options: BFS over words using wildcard patterns
Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly remove in-degree-0 nodes
Union–find with path compression and union by size
BFS gives shortest paths in unweighted graphs
quiz.why: If all nodes get removed there is no cycle.

lessons.title: Lab: Topological order of build steps

scenes.text: A CI pipeline prints a valid order for dependent jobs.
Interviewer: “Works? Good. Now what's the complexity — and can you beat brute force?”

steps.title: Problem
steps.body: Line 1: n m. Next m lines: u v (u must run before v). Print the lexicographically smallest topological order.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.body:
Kahn's algorithm with a min-heap

A heap instead of a queue picks the smallest available node.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Assuming the graph is acyclic without checking.

steps.title: Complexity
steps.body: Time **O((V+E) log V)**, extra space **O(V+E)**. Say both out loud in an interview, then mention the brute force you rejected.

activity.prompt: Line 1: n m. Next m lines: u v (u must run before v). Print the lexicographically smallest topological order.
activity.starter:
import heapq
n, m = map(int, input().split())
E = [tuple(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(m)]
# your code here
activity.solution:
import heapq
n, m = map(int, input().split())
E = [tuple(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(m)]
adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]; indeg = [0] * n
for u, v in E: adj[u].append(v); indeg[v] += 1
h = [i for i in range(n) if indeg[i] == 0]; heapq.heapify(h); out = []
while h:
    u = heapq.heappop(h); out.append(u)
    for v in adj[u]:
        indeg[v] -= 1
        if indeg[v] == 0: heapq.heappush(h, v)
print(*out)

quiz.q: Time complexity of the efficient solution to “Topological order of build steps”?
quiz.why: A heap instead of a queue picks the smallest available node. → O((V+E) log V) time, O(V+E) extra space.

quiz.q:
“Topological order of build steps”: for the input below, what should the program print?
4 3
0 1
0 2
2 3
quiz.why: Trace it: the expected output is 0 1 2 3.

activity.prompt: One line of integers. After each, print the running median (one decimal place).
activity.starter:
import heapq
a = list(map(int, input().split()))
# your code here
activity.solution:
import heapq
a = list(map(int, input().split()))
lo, hi, out = [], [], []
for x in a:
    heapq.heappush(lo, -x); heapq.heappush(hi, -heapq.heappop(lo))
    if len(hi) > len(lo): heapq.heappush(lo, -heapq.heappop(hi))
    m = -lo[0] if len(lo) > len(hi) else (-lo[0] + hi[0]) / 2
    out.append(f'{m:.1f}')
print(*out)

activity.prompt: One lowercase line. Rearrange so no two adjacent chars are equal; print the result (greedy by frequency, ties alphabetical) or -.
activity.starter:
import heapq
s = input().strip()
# your code here
activity.solution:
import heapq
s = input().strip()
from collections import Counter
h = [(-v, ch) for ch, v in Counter(s).items()]; heapq.heapify(h)
out = []; prev = None
while h:
    v, ch = heapq.heappop(h); out.append(ch)
    if prev: heapq.heappush(h, prev)
    prev = (v + 1, ch) if v + 1 < 0 else None
r = ''.join(out)
print(r if len(r) == len(s) else '-')
activity.hint: Hold the last char out for one round.

activity.prompt: One integer n. Print the number of solutions.

n = int(input())
# your code here
activity.solution:
n = int(input())
cols, d1, d2 = set(), set(), set(); cnt = 0
def bt(r):
    global cnt
    if r == n: cnt += 1; return
    for c in range(n):

bt(0); print(cnt)

r, c = map(int, input().split())
g = [list(input().strip()) for _ in range(r)]
w = input().strip()
def dfs(i, j, k):
    if k == len(w): return True
    if not (0 <= i < r and 0 <= j < c) or g[i][j] != w[k]: return False
    t, g[i][j] = g[i][j], '#'
    ok = any(dfs(i + a, j + b, k + 1) for a, b in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)))
    g[i][j] = t; return ok

courses.summary: Three mock interview rounds (coding, pressure scenarios, behavioural), a capstone coding lab and a 20-question final exam across all DSA topics.
outcomes: Learners can perform a structured coding interview
Learners can recover from bugs and blanks calmly
Learners can answer behavioural questions with STAR

scenes.text: The panel joins the video call: one coder, one observer.
45 minutes. Think aloud — they are scoring how you reason.

steps.title: How this round works
steps.body: Five classic problems. Speak your approach, then compare with the model answer.

steps.title: Structure every answer
steps.body:
- Clarify the problem and constraints
- State a brute force, then optimise
- Code cleanly, then test with edge cases
- Give time and space complexity

steps.title: Common interview mistakes
steps.body:
- Coding before clarifying
- Silent thinking for minutes
- Not testing your own code
- Claiming O(n) without justifying it

rounds.q: Given an array of integers and a target, return indices of two numbers adding to target. Optimise beyond O(n^2).
rounds.model: Scan once keeping a hash map from value to index. For each x check whether target − x is already in the map; if so return both indices, else store x. This is O(n) time and O(n) space versus O(n^2) for nested loops. Edge cases: duplicates (3,3 with target 6) work because we check before inserting.
followups: What if the array is sorted?
What if you must return all pairs?

rounds.q: Find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
rounds.model: Use a sliding window with a map of each character's last index. Move right one step at a time; if the character was seen inside the window, jump left to last+1. Track the max window length. Each index enters and leaves once, so O(n) time and O(alphabet) space.
followups: What about at most k distinct characters?

rounds.q: Detect whether a directed graph of course prerequisites has a cycle.
rounds.model: Build adjacency lists and in-degrees, then run Kahn's algorithm: push all in-degree-0 nodes, pop, decrement neighbours. If the processed count is less than n there is a cycle. Alternatively DFS with white/grey/black colours where a grey neighbour means a back edge. O(V+E).
followups: How do you output the actual cycle?

rounds.q: Return the k most frequent elements of an array.
rounds.model: Count frequencies with a hash map, then keep a min-heap of size k keyed by count (O(n log k)), or bucket sort by frequency for O(n). Mention tie-breaking rules and memory use.
followups: What if the data is a stream that doesn't fit in memory?

rounds.q: Coin change: fewest coins to make an amount. Why does greedy fail?
rounds.model: Greedy fails for coins {1,3,4} and amount 6 (greedy 4+1+1 = 3 coins, optimal 3+3 = 2). Use bottom-up DP: dp[0] = 0, dp[x] = min over coins of dp[x−c] + 1. O(coins × amount) time, O(amount) space; return −1 if unreachable.
followups: How do you also return which coins?

tips: Close with how you would verify and monitor.

quiz.q: What should you do first when given a coding problem?
options: Write unit tests for unrelated code
quiz.why: Clarifying prevents solving the wrong problem.

quiz.q: When asked for complexity you should give…
options: Both time and extra space, with a reason
quiz.why: Interviewers expect time and space with justification.

quiz.q: A good way to test your code in an interview is…
options: Walk through a small example and edge cases by hand
Ask the interviewer to test it
quiz.why: Dry runs on small and edge cases catch most bugs.

steps.title: How this round works

rounds.q: Your solution passes the examples but times out on large inputs. What do you do?
rounds.model: Re-read the constraints to find the target complexity, e.g. n = 10^5 means O(n log n) or better. Find the bottleneck — usually a nested loop or repeated work — and replace it with a hash map, prefix sum, heap or two pointers. Re-test edge cases after the change.
followups: What if memory is also limited?

rounds.q: The interviewer says your code has a bug but won't say where. How do you proceed?
rounds.model: Stay calm and dry-run a small input, saying each variable's value out loud. Then try edge cases: empty input, one element, duplicates, negatives, overflow. Check loop bounds and the invariant of each pointer or window. Fix it, then explain what the bug was.

rounds.q: You don't know the optimal approach. What do you say?
rounds.model: Be honest: give the brute force and its complexity first, so there is a working baseline. Then think aloud through patterns — sorting, hashing, two pointers, heaps, DP — and ask whether the constraints allow them. Interviewers score your problem-solving, not only the final answer.

rounds.model: Return the top 5–10 completions for a prefix within ~100 ms p99, ranked by popularity (optionally personalised and localised). API: GET /suggest?q=pyth&lang=en. Freshness of minutes to hours is acceptable.
followups: How fresh must trending terms be?

rounds.q: How do you store and query prefixes fast?
rounds.model: Use a trie where each node stores a precomputed top-k list of completions, so a lookup is O(length of prefix). Serve it from memory in sharded suggestion servers, with a CDN/edge cache for very common short prefixes.

rounds.q: How do you build and update rankings?
rounds.model: Aggregate search logs in batch (hourly/daily) to counts with decay, rebuild tries offline, and atomically swap them into servers. For trending, a streaming job (e.g. Kafka + Flink) updates a small overlay of hot terms.
followups: How do you handle offensive terms?

rounds.model: Shard by prefix ranges sized by traffic, not alphabet, because 's' is hotter than 'x'. Replicate each shard for availability and read throughput; route with a lightweight routing table.

If a shard is down, serve from replicas or a stale cache, and degrade to no suggestions rather than block search. Monitor p99 latency, cache hit rate and suggestion click-through, and apply a blocklist filter.

tips: Drive the conversation; check in with the interviewer.

quiz.q: Core data structure for typeahead?
Why shard by traffic-weighted prefix ranges?
How are rankings refreshed?
options: Offline rebuild from logs + streaming overlay for trends

rounds.model: Send notifications over push, SMS and email from many internal services, with templates, user preferences/opt-outs, scheduling, rate limits per user, and at-least-once delivery with deduplication. Scale: say 100M notifications/day.

rounds.model: API get(key)/put(key, value) with low latency at large scale. Under network partitions we must choose availability or consistency (CAP); a Dynamo-style store chooses availability with tunable consistency per request.
Consistent hashing on a ring with virtual nodes spreads keys evenly and moves only ~1/N of keys when a node joins or leaves.

Replicate each key to N successors on the ring. With read quorum R and write quorum W, R + W > N gives read-your-latest-write overlap (e.g. N=3, R=2, W=2). Sloppy quorum with hinted handoff keeps writes available during failures.

Detect concurrent versions with vector clocks (or use last-write-wins with synchronized clocks if acceptable), fix stale replicas with read repair, and run background anti-entropy using Merkle trees to compare ranges cheaply.
Writes go to a commit log and memtable, flushed to immutable SSTables (LSM tree) with compaction and Bloom filters for reads. Nodes share membership and failure information via gossip.

tips: Drive the conversation; check in with the interviewer.

rounds.model: Crawl about 1 billion pages a month, respect robots.txt and per-host politeness, avoid duplicates, prioritise important/fresh pages, and store raw HTML for indexing. 1B/month ≈ 400 pages/s average.

A URL frontier (priority + per-host queues) feeds distributed fetchers with a DNS cache; fetched pages go to a parser that extracts links, to a dedupe step, and to a content store (object storage) for indexing.

rounds.model: Limit depth/URL length and pages per host to escape infinite calendars or session-ID traps; time out slow servers; checkpoint the frontier so crashed workers resume.

rounds.model: Users upload videos; we transcode them and stream globally with adaptive bitrate, low start-up time and high availability; plus metadata, search and approximate view counts.

Clients upload directly to object storage with pre-signed (resumable, multipart) URLs. An event triggers a processing DAG: validate, transcode to several renditions in parallel chunks, generate thumbnails, run moderation, then publish manifests.
The player fetches an HLS/DASH manifest and small segments from the CDN, switching bitrate with bandwidth. Popular videos are cached at the edge; long-tail content is fetched from origin storage.
Video metadata in a replicated DB behind a cache; view counts aggregated asynchronously from playback events through a stream processor, accepting eventual consistency.
Move cold renditions to cheaper storage tiers, transcode rare resolutions lazily, use multi-CDN for resilience, and make transcoding chunks idempotent so failed chunks retry independently.

rounds.q: How do you find nearby drivers?

Send offers to the best few drivers; atomically reserve a driver (e.g. compare-and-set on driver state) so two riders can't get the same one; time out unanswered offers. Trips follow a state machine stored durably.
Shard by city/region, scale hot cells (stadium after a match), apply surge pricing to balance supply, and fail over regionally with trip state replicated.

steps.title: The 7-step frame
steps.body:
1. Functional & non-functional requirements
2. Back-of-envelope estimates

rounds.model: Users upload files, sync them across devices (including offline edits), share them, and see version history. Durability must be extremely high; sync latency of seconds is fine.
Split files into chunks (e.g. 4 MB) addressed by hash and stored in object storage; a metadata DB stores files, versions (lists of chunk hashes), folders and permissions.

The client detects changes, hashes chunks, asks the server which chunks are missing, uploads only those, then commits a new version. Other devices get a notification (WebSocket/long poll) and download the changed chunks.
If two devices edit the same base version offline, the second commit detects the mismatch and the server keeps both: a 'conflicted copy' for the user to resolve. Never silently overwrite.
Store chunks with replication or erasure coding across zones, encrypt at rest and in transit, and check permissions on every metadata and chunk access via signed URLs.

tips: Drive the conversation; check in with the interviewer.

quiz.q: Uploading only missing chunks is called…

options: A conflicted copy, not silent overwrite

quiz.q: Erasure coding offers…
options: High durability with less storage than full replication

rounds.model: Accept payments through external PSPs, never double-charge, keep an auditable ledger, handle refunds, reconcile daily with PSP reports, and minimise PCI scope by tokenising cards via the PSP.

Create a payment intent with an idempotency key, call the PSP, and move through a state machine (created → pending → succeeded/failed) driven by synchronous responses and asynchronous webhooks, which are verified and idempotently processed.
Use a double-entry, append-only ledger: every movement debits one account and credits another, entries are immutable, and balances are derived; corrections are new entries.
On a timeout the state is unknown — never blindly retry with a new key. Query the PSP or retry with the same idempotency key, and let daily reconciliation catch any mismatch.
Publish PaymentSucceeded via a transactional outbox; the order service confirms the order; if fulfilment fails, a saga compensates with a refund.

tips: Drive the conversation; check in with the interviewer.

ticket.short: 3 payments failed internally but captured at PSP
ticket.description: Recon report 25 Nov: PSP shows 3 captured payments (₹12,480 total) that our system marked FAILED. Customers were charged but orders cancelled.

investigate.label: Payment logs for the 3 intents
investigate.reveal: All 3 hit a 30 s client timeout calling the PSP at 21:14–21:16; code marked them FAILED on timeout.

investigate.label: Webhook logs
investigate.reveal: PSP webhooks 'payment.captured' arrived at 21:17 but were rejected: signature check failed after a key rotation that evening.

investigate.label: Customer device types
investigate.reveal: Mixed Android/iOS — irrelevant.

investigate.label: DB replication lag
investigate.reveal: Normal (< 1 s).

options: Timeouts treated as failures, and webhooks rejected after a signing-key rotation
diagnosis.why: Unknown outcomes were finalised as FAILED, and the correcting webhooks were dropped due to the stale signing key.

resolution: Update the webhook signing secret and replay the 3 webhooks
Mark the payments SUCCEEDED, restore or refund orders per customer choice
Change timeout handling to PENDING + status poll, never FAILED
Alert on webhook signature failures
Add a key-rotation runbook step to update all verifiers

closure.model: Root cause: PSP calls timed out and were marked FAILED; PSP 'captured' webhooks were rejected because the signing key was rotated without updating our verifier. Fix: updated secret, replayed webhooks, reconciled 3 orders (2 restored, 1 refunded). Prevention: timeouts → PENDING with status polling; alert on signature failures; rotation runbook. Verified: next recon shows 0 mismatches.

rounds.model: Users browse shows, view a seat map, hold seats for a few minutes, pay, and get tickets. No seat may be sold twice; must survive flash crowds when popular shows open.

Model each seat-show as a row with state (available/held/booked). Hold with an atomic conditional update (`UPDATE … SET state='held', hold_until=… WHERE state='available'`) or Redis SET NX with TTL; confirm after payment with a unique constraint on (show, seat).
Put a virtual waiting room in front, rate-limit per user, cache the read-heavy seat map with short TTLs and push updates, and shard by show/venue.
Holds expire automatically; payment uses idempotency keys; on success confirm seats, on failure or timeout release holds (saga with compensation).
Limit seats per user, detect bots (rate patterns, CAPTCHA), and keep an audit trail of holds and bookings.

rounds.model: Collect metrics from thousands of services, store time series efficiently, support queries/dashboards and reliable alerting, with high-resolution recent data and downsampled long-term retention.
Pull (scrape) via service discovery suits long-lived services; push via agents/gateways suits short-lived jobs. Each series is a metric name plus labels.
Use a time-series database writing in-memory head blocks then immutable compressed blocks (delta-of-delta timestamps, XOR floats), with downsampling and tiered retention to object storage.
High-cardinality labels (user_id, request_id) explode the number of series and memory; enforce label limits and use logs/traces for per-request data.
Evaluate rules close to the data, deduplicate and route alerts (Alertmanager-like), and monitor the monitoring with a heartbeat ('dead man's switch') alert from outside.

tips: Drive the conversation; check in with the interviewer.

rounds.q: Design a URL shortener's analytics pipeline that counts clicks per link per hour.
rounds.model: Emit click events to a log (Kafka), aggregate per link per hour in a stream processor with windowing and late-event handling, write aggregates to an OLAP store (e.g. ClickHouse/Druid) and serve dashboards from it. Raw events go to cheap storage for reprocessing.

rounds.q: How would you design a global rate limiter for an API with 10 regions?
rounds.model: Use token buckets enforced locally in each region for low latency, with periodic synchronisation of counts to a global budget (approximate, eventually consistent). Strict global limits cost a cross-region round trip, so reserve them for expensive operations.

rounds.q: Design a leaderboard for a mobile game with 50M players.
rounds.model: Redis sorted sets give O(log n) updates and top-k reads; shard by game/season, keep a global top-1000 merged from shard tops, and approximate ranks for the long tail with score histograms.

rounds.q: Design a distributed job scheduler (cron at scale).
rounds.model: Store job definitions and next-run times in a durable DB; partition by job ID across scheduler nodes with leases; enqueue due jobs to a queue for workers with heartbeats and retries; require idempotent jobs since delivery is at-least-once.

rounds.q: Design a news-feed ranking upgrade without hurting latency.
rounds.model: Split into candidate generation (fan-out-on-write for most users, fan-out-on-read for celebrities) and a ranking service with a latency budget; precompute features, cache results, A/B test, and fall back to chronological ranking if the ranker is slow.

rounds.q: You estimated 10k QPS but launch traffic is 100k QPS. What breaks first and what do you do?
rounds.model: Typically the database or its connection pool saturates first, then latency cascades. Immediately shed or rate-limit non-critical traffic, scale stateless tiers out, add caching for hot reads, and add read replicas; longer term shard or redesign hot paths.

rounds.q: The interviewer pushes: 'Why not just use one big SQL database?'

rounds.q: Tell me about a system you designed and a trade-off you regret.
rounds.model: Use STAR: e.g. we chose eventual consistency for inventory to scale, which caused oversells during sales; we added reservations with TTLs. Lesson: model contention hotspots explicitly.

courses.title: vSphere HA: design & operations
courses.summary: How vSphere HA detects failures and restarts VMs: FDM primary/secondary, network and datastore heartbeats, isolation response, admission control, restart priorities, VM monitoring and VMCP.
outcomes: Learners can explain FDM roles and heartbeats

lessons.title: How HA decides a host failed

scenes.text: esx07 lost both power supplies at 03:12. By 03:15 its VMs were running on other hosts.
Who decided, and how?

steps.title: FDM
steps.body: Each host runs the **FDM** agent. One host is elected **primary**; the others are secondaries. The primary monitors secondaries via **network heartbeats** (management vmk) and **datastore heartbeats** (by default 2 heartbeat datastores).

steps.title: Three situations
steps.body:
- **Failed**: no network or datastore heartbeats and no ping response → restart its VMs elsewhere.
- **Isolated**: host is alive but cannot reach other hosts nor its **isolation address** (default gateway) → applies the **isolation response** (Disabled, Shut down and restart VMs, Power off and restart VMs).
- **Partitioned**: groups of hosts can't talk to each other but each group is still up; a new primary may be elected per partition.

steps.title: HA is not zero downtime
steps.body: HA **restarts** VMs (minutes of downtime; guest reboots). For zero-downtime of a single VM, Fault Tolerance exists with strict limits. Applications still need their own clustering for app-level failures.

activity.prompt: Failed, isolated or partitioned?

items.text: No network or datastore heartbeats, no ping response
Host can't ping peers or its gateway, but still updates heartbeat datastores
Hosts 1–3 see each other; hosts 4–6 see each other; the groups can't talk

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Tolerating 1 of 5 identical hosts → reserve **1/5 = 20%** CPU and memory. vSphere computes this automatically from 'Host failures cluster tolerates' (in vSphere 6.5+). With 2 failures tolerated: 40%.

steps.title: Policies
steps.body:
- **Cluster resource percentage** (default, flexible).
- **Slot policy** (based on largest reservations; conservative).
- **Dedicated failover hosts** (idle standby hosts).
- **Performance degradation VMs tolerate** warns if failover would degrade performance beyond a threshold.

courses.title: DRS, affinity rules & resource pools
courses.summary: Balance clusters with DRS: automation levels, migration threshold, affinity/anti-affinity rules, shares/reservations/limits, and the resource-pool share-dilution trap.
outcomes: Learners can configure DRS automation and threshold
Learners can write VM-VM and VM-host rules
Learners can calculate shares and entitlement
Learners can diagnose the resource-pool dilution problem

scenes.text: esx01 sits at 92% CPU while esx04 idles at 20%.
DRS should fix that — but it's set to Manual.

steps.title: Automation levels
steps.body:
- **Manual**: recommendations only.
- **Partially automated**: automatic initial placement; migrations are recommendations.
- **Fully automated**: placement and migrations automatic.
Migration threshold 1 (conservative) … 5 (aggressive); default 3. Since vSphere 7, DRS optimises a per-VM **DRS score** (how well each VM gets its resources).

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- VM-VM **affinity** (keep together) and **anti-affinity** (keep apart, e.g. two domain controllers).
- VM-Host rules: **must** / **should** run (or not run) on a host group.
Use 'should' unless there is a hard licensing or compliance reason.

steps.title: Predictive & other features
steps.body: DRS also does initial placement at power-on and works with maintenance mode evacuation.

pairs: Keep DC01 and DC02 on different hosts

scenes.text: Cluster has 100 GHz CPU. Pool Prod: High shares; pool Dev: Low shares. Both busy.
Who gets what under contention?

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Shares**: relative priority *only under contention*. High:Normal:Low = **4:2:1**.
- **Reservation**: guaranteed minimum.
- **Limit**: hard cap (even if resources are free!).
- **Expandable reservation**: a pool may borrow reservation from its parent.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Prod High (4) vs Dev Low (1) → Prod gets 4/5 = **80 GHz**, Dev 1/5 = **20 GHz** when both demand everything.

courses.title: CPU performance: ready, co-stop & right-sizing
courses.summary: Read CPU performance like an expert: %RDY, %CSTP, %MLMTD in esxtop, vCenter ready summation maths, NUMA, and right-sizing tickets.
outcomes: Learners can convert ready summation to percent
Learners can read esxtop CPU counters

story.title: 'The VM is slow but CPU is only 40%'

scenes.text: Guest Task Manager shows 40% CPU, yet users complain.
The hypervisor's view tells the truth.

steps.title: Counters
steps.body:
- **%USED / %RUN**: time vCPUs ran.
- **%RDY (ready)**: time a vCPU was ready to run but waited for a physical CPU → contention.
- **%CSTP (co-stop)**: time vCPUs were held to keep sibling vCPUs in step → often oversized VMs.
- **%MLMTD**: time not run due to a CPU **limit**.
- **%WAIT / %IDLE**: waiting (I/O or idle).

steps.title: Rules of thumb
steps.body: Per vCPU: %RDY above ~5% deserves a look, above ~10% usually hurts. %CSTP above ~3% suggests too many vCPUs. In esxtop, the VM row aggregates all vCPUs — expand (press **e**) or divide by vCPU count.

steps.title: vCenter ready summation
steps.body: Real-time charts sample every **20 s** (20,000 ms). Ready % = summation ms ÷ 20,000 × 100. E.g. 2,000 ms → 10% for the whole VM; for a 4-vCPU VM ≈ 2.5% per vCPU.

steps.title: NUMA
steps.body: Each socket has its local memory (a NUMA node). A VM that fits inside one node (≤16 vCPU and ≤ node memory here) gets local memory access. Keep cores-per-socket aligned with physical topology (vSphere 8 sets sensible defaults automatically for new VMs).

courses.title: Memory management: TPS, ballooning, compression & swap
courses.summary: How ESXi reclaims memory, which counters prove pressure, why limits cause ballooning on idle hosts, and how to fix swapping incidents.
outcomes: Learners can order reclamation techniques by cost
Learners can read esxtop memory counters
Learners can explain host memory states
Learners can resolve a ballooning/swapping ticket

scenes.text: Cluster has 1 TB RAM but 1.3 TB configured to VMs.
ESXi uses several techniques before trouble starts.

steps.title: From cheap to expensive
steps.body:
1. **Transparent Page Sharing (TPS)**: dedupes identical pages; by default **within a VM only** (inter-VM sharing disabled by default for security since 2014 'salting').
2. **Ballooning**: VMware Tools balloon driver (vmmemctl) asks the guest to give back memory; guest chooses what to page out.
3. **Memory compression**: compress pages into a per-VM cache instead of swapping.
4. **Hypervisor swapping** to .vswp: slowest; host picks pages without guest knowledge.
(Host swap cache on SSD can soften swapping.)

steps.title: Host memory states
steps.body: High → Clear → Soft → Hard → Low as free memory falls; reclamation becomes more aggressive at each step (ballooning first, compression/swapping in hard/low).

steps.title: Limits again
steps.body: A VM **memory limit** below its configured RAM causes ballooning/swap even when the host has plenty free. It is a classic hidden misconfiguration.

courses.title: Storage & network performance with esxtop
courses.summary: Find storage latency (DAVG/KAVG/GAVG/QAVG), queue depth problems, and network drops with esxtop and vCenter charts; resolve a noisy-neighbour ticket.
outcomes: Learners can interpret storage latency layers
Learners can identify queueing and noisy neighbours

scenes.text: Users say 'the disk is slow'. But which layer?
esxtop splits it up.

steps.title: Layers
steps.body:
- **DAVG**: device/array latency (fabric + array).
- **KAVG**: time in the VMkernel (should be ~0–1 ms); includes **QAVG** queueing.
- **GAVG** ≈ DAVG + KAVG: what the guest sees.
Rules of thumb: DAVG consistently > 20 ms is poor for most workloads; KAVG > 2 ms indicates host-side queueing.

steps.title: Queue depth
steps.body: Each HBA and device has a queue depth (DQLEN). If many VMs share one LUN, the device queue fills → QAVG rises. Fixes: spread VMs across datastores, adjust queue depth per vendor guidance, enable **Storage I/O Control (SIOC)** to share fairly under contention.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Blaming the array when KAVG is high (host-side), or raising queue depth without vendor guidance.

courses.title: Backup & recovery for vSphere
courses.summary: Protect vSphere properly: VADP and CBT, application consistency, 3-2-1-1-0, immutability against ransomware, vCenter file-based backup, restore testing, and a failing-backup ticket.
outcomes: Learners can explain VADP, CBT and quiescing
Learners can set RPO/RTO-based policies
Learners can protect vCenter itself
Learners can troubleshoot a failing VM backup

scenes.text: The backup tool takes a snapshot every night — so are snapshots backups after all?
No: the snapshot is only a temporary freeze so data can be copied elsewhere.

steps.title: VADP flow
steps.body: Backup software uses the **vSphere Storage APIs – Data Protection (VADP)**: 1) take a (quiesced) snapshot, 2) read the frozen base disk via transport (hot-add, NBD/NBDSSL, SAN), 3) use **Changed Block Tracking (CBT)** to copy only changed blocks for incrementals, 4) delete the snapshot.

steps.title: Consistency
steps.body:
- Crash-consistent: like pulling power.
- **Application-consistent**: VMware Tools/VSS quiesces apps (SQL, Exchange) before the snapshot.
Databases may also need log truncation handled by the backup tool.

steps.title: Policy
steps.body: **RPO** = how much data you can lose (time). **RTO** = how fast you must restore. **3-2-1-1-0**: 3 copies, 2 media, 1 offsite, 1 offline/immutable, 0 errors in restore tests.

activity.prompt: Match term to meaning.
pairs: APIs backup tools use to read VM disks
Tracks changed blocks for fast incrementals
Can't be altered/deleted for a retention period

options: At most 4 hours of data may be lost

quiz.q: Best defence against ransomware deleting backups?

options: Backup proxy VM mounts the snapshot disks directly

scenes.text: VMs keep running, but no HA config changes, no DRS, no backups that depend on vCenter.
Protect the appliance.

steps.title: Options
steps.body:
- **File-based backup** from VAMI (:5480) to SFTP/FTPS/HTTPS/NFS/SMB on a schedule; restore by deploying a new VCSA from ISO and choosing Restore.
- Image-level backup of the VCSA VM is possible but file-based is the documented path.
- Keep backups of distributed switch configs (export) and note SSO/AD details.

tech-vmw-foundations.description: Zero-to-admin vSphere 8 foundations: virtualization concepts, ESXi install and esxcli, vCenter, access control and Day-1 host configuration, with simulated consoles and real-world tickets. Independent learning material; not affiliated with VMware or Broadcom.

courses.title: Virtualization concepts for administrators
courses.summary: From zero: what a hypervisor really does, how CPU, memory, storage and network are shared, and why companies consolidate onto vSphere. Note: VMware is now part of Broadcom (acquisition completed in late 2023); the technology covered here is vSphere 8.
outcomes: Learners can explain type-1 vs type-2 hypervisors and where ESXi fits
Learners can describe how vCPU, vRAM, virtual disks and virtual NICs map to physical resources
Learners can size a basic consolidation with N+1 headroom
Learners can pitch benefits and limits of virtualization honestly

lessons.title: How a hypervisor shares one server

story.title: The server room nobody could cool

scenes.text: Contoso's old server room has 40 physical servers, most of them below 15% CPU. The air-conditioning bill is enormous.
Ravi, the new infra lead, proposes running those workloads as virtual machines on four ESXi hosts.

steps.title: What is a hypervisor?
steps.body:
A **hypervisor** is a thin layer of software that creates and runs **virtual machines (VMs)**. Each VM believes it has its own CPU, memory, disk and network card.

- **Type 1 (bare-metal)** runs directly on hardware: ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM.
- **Type 2 (hosted)** runs as an app on a normal OS: VMware Workstation, VirtualBox.

ESXi is type 1: the VMkernel schedules CPU, manages memory and owns the drivers.

steps.title: How resources map
steps.body:
- **vCPU**: a scheduling slot; the VMkernel places it on a physical core/thread when the VM needs to run.
- **vRAM**: guest 'physical' memory, backed by host RAM (and, under pressure, by balloon, compression or swap).
- **Virtual disk (VMDK)**: a file on a datastore (VMFS, NFS, vSAN, vVols).
- **vNIC**: connects to a port group on a virtual switch, which uplinks to physical NICs.

Hardware assistance (Intel VT-x / AMD-V, EPT/RVI) lets guests run most instructions at near-native speed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking more vCPUs always = faster. Over-sized VMs wait longer to be scheduled.
- Forgetting that a host failure now takes down *many* workloads: you need HA and spare capacity.
- Treating snapshots as backups (they are not; covered later).

activity.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Virtual disk file on a datastore
Virtual processor scheduled on physical cores
Network policy/VLAN that vNICs attach to
ESXi's core OS: scheduler, memory, drivers

quiz.q: Why can over-allocating vCPUs to a VM hurt performance?

quiz.q: What does hardware-assisted virtualization (VT-x/AMD-V) provide?

steps.title: Physical vs virtual objects

Physical: hosts, CPUs, DIMMs, HBAs, pNICs (vmnic0…), LUNs on the array.

Virtual: VMs, vNICs, VMDKs, port groups, vSwitches, VMkernel adapters (vmk0…), resource pools.

steps.title: Workloads that need care
steps.body: Most workloads virtualize well. Extra planning is needed for: licence-dongle USB devices, very latency-sensitive trading or telecom apps, GPU-heavy work (needs vGPU/passthrough), and software whose licence is tied to physical cores.

steps.title: Ask the right question

lessons.title: Lab: Size a consolidation with N+1

story.title: How many hosts do we buy?

scenes.text: Finance asks Ravi for a number by Friday.
Monitoring shows 40 servers, each 4 cores, averaging 25% busy. New hosts have 32 cores and the team plans to run them at no more than 70% CPU.

steps.title: Worked method
steps.body:
1. Demand = 40 × 4 cores × 25% = **40 cores** of real work.
2. Usable per host = 32 × 70% = **22.4 cores**.
3. Hosts for load = 40 ÷ 22.4 = 1.79 → round up to **2**.
4. Add **N+1** so one host can fail or be patched: **3 hosts**.

Repeat the same maths for memory; the bigger answer wins.

steps.title: Memory check
steps.body: 40 servers using 12 GB each = 480 GB. Hosts with 512 GB, planned to 80% = 409.6 GB usable → 480 ÷ 409.6 = 1.17 → 2 hosts, +1 = 3. CPU and RAM agree on 3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sizing on peaks of every server at once (over-buys) or on averages without headroom (under-buys).
- Forgetting growth (add 20–30% for 3 years) and N+1.
- Ignoring that maintenance windows also remove a host.

activity.prompt: Workload: 60 servers × 8 cores at 20% average CPU. New hosts: 48 cores, run at max 75% CPU. How many hosts including N+1? (CPU only)

Why add N+1?
options: So workloads still fit when one host fails or is in maintenance
Because vCenter needs a spare host
quiz.why: HA needs spare capacity to restart VMs.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — pitch virtualization to the CIO

scenes.text: The CIO says: 'Convince me. And tell me what can go wrong.'

steps.title: Benefits
steps.body:
- Consolidation: fewer servers, power, cooling, rack space.
- Mobility: vMotion for maintenance without downtime.
- Availability: HA restarts VMs after host failure.
- Speed: templates deploy a VM in minutes.

steps.title: Risks to own
steps.body:
- Bigger blast radius per host → HA, N+1, monitoring.
- Shared storage becomes critical → redundant paths, capacity alerts.
- Sprawl: VMs are easy to create and forget → lifecycle rules.
- Licensing costs and terms change over time; review with your vendor.

steps.body: Translate tech to outcomes: 'patch hosts in business hours with zero downtime' beats 'we will use vMotion'.

choices.label: Say 'everyone uses VMware, so we should'
choices.feedback: Weak argument; give outcomes and numbers.

choices.label: Name the risks (blast radius, storage dependency, sprawl, licensing) and the controls for each
Say there is no risk
choices.feedback: The CIO knows that is not true.

courses.title: ESXi installation & first configuration
courses.summary: Prepare hardware, install ESXi 8, configure the management network, DNS, NTP and hostname, and fix the classic 'new host unreachable' problem.
outcomes: Learners can check hardware readiness (compatibility guide, BIOS settings, boot media)

story.title: Three new servers on the loading dock

scenes.text: Three new rack servers arrive for the Pune DC. The install is booked for tonight.
Ananya, the vSphere admin, runs her readiness checklist first.

steps.title: What to check
steps.body:
- Server model, CPU, NIC and storage controller listed in the **VMware Compatibility Guide** for ESXi 8.
- BIOS/UEFI: **VT-x/AMD-V enabled**, execute-disable (NX/XD) on, power profile set to OS-controlled or high performance as per your standard.
- Boot device: ESXi 8 needs a persistent boot device of at least **32 GB**; **128 GB** or more is recommended. SD-card/USB-only boot is deprecated.
- Firmware at vendor-recommended levels, out-of-band management (iDRAC/iLO/XCC) reachable.

steps.title: Network plan before you start
steps.body: Have ready: management IP, mask, gateway, VLAN ID, DNS servers, FQDN (with forward and reverse DNS records), NTP servers and root password policy.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: No reverse DNS record (vCenter add-host problems later), management VLAN not trunked on the switch port, or virtualization disabled in BIOS.

Firmware/BIOS at vendor-recommended version

story.title: The intern who could delete production

scenes.text: An intern was added to 'Administrators' at vCenter root 'just for a week'.

steps.title: Building blocks
steps.body:
- **Principal**: a user or group from an identity source (vsphere.local, Active Directory over LDAPS, or identity federation e.g. ADFS/Entra ID).
- **Privilege**: a single action (e.g. *Virtual machine > Interaction > Power on*).
- **Role**: a named set of privileges (Administrator, Read-only, No access, custom roles).
- **Permission**: principal + role assigned on an object, optionally **propagated** to children.

steps.title: Rules of thumb
steps.body:
- A permission set on a child object overrides the one inherited from the parent.
- If a user is in several groups with permissions on the same object, the privileges combine.
- **No access** explicitly blocks.
- **Global permissions** apply across all vCenters in the SSO domain and to solutions like tags/content libraries.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Granting Administrator to individuals instead of AD groups; forgetting 'Propagate to children'; using the SSO administrator account for daily work.

statements.s: A role is a collection of privileges.
A permission assigned on a VM folder never affects VMs inside it.
A permission defined directly on a child object overrides an inherited one.
statements.why: Explicit on child wins over inherited.

statements.s: Using administrator@vsphere.local for daily tasks is best practice.
statements.why: Use named AD accounts; keep the SSO admin for break-glass.

statements.s: The 'No access' role can block a user from an object.

options: Assign roles to AD groups, least privilege

options: All vCenters in the SSO domain and global objects like tags

tech-vmw-network-storage.title: VMware vSphere 2: Networking & Storage
tech-vmw-network-storage.description: vSphere 8 networking and storage, hands-on: standard and distributed switches, VMFS, NFS, iSCSI, vSAN and multipathing, with simulated esxcli/PowerCLI consoles and real incident tickets. Independent learning material; not affiliated with VMware or Broadcom.

courses.title: Standard switches (vSS) & VMkernel networking
courses.summary: Build per-host standard switches, port groups, VLAN tagging, NIC teaming and VMkernel adapters, and test jumbo frames end-to-end.
outcomes: Learners can explain vSS, port groups, uplinks and VMkernel adapters
Learners can choose VLAN tagging mode (EST/VST/VGT) and teaming policy
Learners can build a vSwitch with esxcli
Learners can troubleshoot an MTU mismatch with vmkping

scenes.text: A packet leaves web01's vNIC. Fatima, the network admin, asks the vSphere team: 'which cable does it use?'
They draw: vNIC → port group → vSwitch → uplink vmnic → physical switch port.

steps.title: Pieces
steps.body:
- **vSphere Standard Switch (vSS)**: configured per host; each host must be set up identically.
- **Port group**: policy container (VLAN ID, security, teaming, shaping) that VM vNICs connect to.
- **VMkernel adapter (vmkN)**: host's own IP interface; enable services per adapter: Management, vMotion, Provisioning, Fault Tolerance logging, vSAN, vSphere Replication, NVMe over TCP/RDMA.
- **Uplinks**: physical NICs (vmnicN). A vSwitch does not forward between its uplinks, so it cannot create a loop like a bridging switch.

steps.title: VLAN tagging modes
steps.body:
- **EST** (VLAN ID 0): physical switch tags; port is access.
- **VST** (1–4094): vSwitch tags; physical port is a trunk. Most common.
- **VGT** (4095 on vSS): the guest OS tags; use for appliances that need many VLANs.

steps.title: Teaming (load balancing)
steps.body: Route based on originating virtual port (default), source MAC hash, IP hash (requires a static EtherChannel on the physical switch), explicit failover order. Plus failover detection (link status or beacon probing) and notify switches.

activity.prompt: Match the setting to its meaning.
pairs: VLAN ID 4095 on a vSS port group
Guest tagging (VGT): trunk to the VM
Needs static EtherChannel on the physical switch
Dedicated VMkernel adapter for live migration
Default teaming: each vNIC pinned to one uplink

quiz.q: Most common tagging in enterprises?
IP hash teaming requires…
options: A static EtherChannel/port-channel on the physical switch
quiz.why: vSS supports static EtherChannel, not LACP.

quiz.q: Can a vSS create a layer-2 loop between its uplinks?
options: No, it does not forward frames between uplinks
quiz.why: Hence no STP needed on vSS.

quiz.q: Which is configured per host?

courses.title: Distributed switches (vDS)
courses.summary: Centralised networking with vDS: architecture, features (LACP, NIOC, LBT, port mirroring, health check), PowerCLI build, safe migration from vSS, and a teaming-mismatch ticket.
outcomes: Learners can explain vDS control vs data plane and features beyond vSS
Learners can plan a safe vSS→vDS migration
Learners can create a vDS and port groups with PowerCLI
Learners can troubleshoot teaming/LACP mismatches

scenes.text: Configuring 12 standard switches by hand caused 3 outages last year.
The team moves to a vSphere Distributed Switch.

steps.title: Architecture
steps.body: The vDS is **defined in vCenter** (management plane); each host keeps a hidden copy (**data plane**) that forwards traffic even if vCenter is down. Port groups are **distributed port groups**; uplinks are abstracted as Uplink1..N mapped to vmnics per host.

steps.title: Features beyond vSS
steps.body:
- LACP (dynamic link aggregation)
- Route based on physical NIC load (**LBT**)
- Network I/O Control (NIOC) shares/reservations per traffic type
- Port mirroring, NetFlow (IPFIX), private VLANs
- Health check (VLAN/MTU and teaming)

story.title: Why is the datastore 'full' when the VMs are small?

scenes.text: Tanvi sees a 4 TB datastore with 12 VMs that 'only use 900 GB'.
Provisioned and used space are different things.

steps.title: VMFS-6
steps.body: Clustered file system: many hosts mount the same LUN; on-disk locking (ATS on VAAI arrays) prevents two hosts writing the same VM files. Max datastore 64 TB, VMDK up to 62 TB, 1 MB file block size, **automatic space reclamation (UNMAP)**, support for 512e and 4Kn devices.

steps.title: Disk formats
steps.body:
- **Thin**: grows as written; saves space; risk of datastore running full.
- **Thick lazy-zeroed**: space allocated now, zeroed on first write.
- **Thick eager-zeroed**: allocated and zeroed upfront; required for some clustering (e.g. shared disks) and Fault Tolerance.

Arrays with thin provisioning add a second layer: watch both.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Overcommitting thin disks without alarms; forgetting snapshot deltas and .vswp (swap = configured RAM − reservation) also consume datastore space.

activity.prompt: Match the format to its property.
pairs: Allocates blocks as the guest writes
Allocated upfront, zeroed on first write
VM swap = configured memory minus reservation

scenes.text: Tanvi must report risk on DS-PURE-03 (8 TB).
Sum of provisioned VMDKs is 14 TB; actually written is 5.6 TB.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Overcommit ratio = provisioned ÷ capacity = 14 ÷ 8 = **1.75 : 1** (175%).
Used = 5.6 ÷ 8 = **70%**.
Free = 2.4 TB. If guests grow 200 GB/month, months to full ≈ 2.4 ÷ 0.2 = **12** (minus snapshot and swap headroom).

steps.title: Policy
steps.body: Common practice: alarm at 75–80% used, critical at 85–90%, and cap overcommit (e.g. ≤ 150%) for production tiers.

lessons.title: NFS on ESXi: v3 vs v4.1

scenes.text: The team wants an NFS share on the NAS (10.10.40.20) for ISOs and templates.
Which NFS version?

steps.title: Facts
steps.body:
- **NFS 3**: single connection per datastore, AUTH_SYS, ESXi needs root access (no root squash) on the export.
- **NFS 4.1**: session trunking (multipathing), Kerberos (krb5/krb5i) optional, better locking.
- Do **not** mount the same export as NFS 3 on some hosts and 4.1 on others (different locking → corruption risk).
- NFS datastores are file-level; the NAS owns the filesystem (no VMFS).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Root squash on the export (read-only/permission denied), mounting via different names/IPs on different hosts (seen as different datastores), VMkernel on the wrong subnet.

ESXi formats NFS datastores with VMFS.

scenes.text: Array portals 10.10.50.10 and .11 on a single subnet; host has vmk4 and vmk5 each pinned to one uplink.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:
1. `esxcli iscsi software set --enabled=true`
2. `esxcli iscsi adapter list` (find vmhba, e.g. vmhba64)
3. Port binding: `esxcli iscsi networkportal add -A vmhba64 -n vmk4` (and vmk5). Each vmk must have exactly **one active uplink, no standby**.
4. Discovery: `esxcli iscsi adapter discovery sendtarget add -A vmhba64 -a 10.10.50.10:3260`
5. `esxcli storage core adapter rescan -A vmhba64`

steps.title: When NOT to bind
steps.body: Port binding is for targets reachable on the same subnet as the bound vmks. If portals are in different routed subnets, don't bind; use separate vmks per subnet.

scenes.text: The SAN contract renews next year. The CIO asks about vSAN.

steps.title: What vSAN is
steps.body: vSAN pools local SSD/NVMe across cluster hosts into one **vsanDatastore**. Objects (VMDK, namespace, swap) are split into components placed on different hosts by a **storage policy**. Needs a VMkernel adapter tagged for vSAN on each host (10 GbE+; ESA needs 25 GbE+).

steps.title: OSA vs ESA
steps.body:
- **OSA** (Original Storage Architecture): **disk groups** = 1 cache device + 1–7 capacity devices.
- **ESA** (Express Storage Architecture, vSphere 8): single-tier **storage pool** of NVMe devices, no cache tier, more efficient RAID-5/6 and compression by default.
- Minimum 3 hosts for a standard cluster; 2-node clusters use a **witness** appliance.

steps.title: Policies (OSA)
steps.body:
FTT = failures to tolerate.
- FTT=1 RAID-1: 2 copies + witness → **3 hosts**, 2× capacity.
- FTT=1 RAID-5: **4 hosts**, 1.33×.
- FTT=2 RAID-1: **5 hosts**, 3×.
- FTT=2 RAID-6: **6 hosts**, 1.5×.

scenes.text: 40 VMs × 250 GB = 10 TB of VMDK.
Policy FTT=1 RAID-5 (OSA), keep 25–30% slack for rebuilds and operations.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Usable data 10 TB × 1.33 (RAID-5 3+1) = **13.3 TB** raw. With 30% slack: 13.3 ÷ 0.7 = **19 TB** raw needed across the cluster (before dedupe/compression savings).

steps.title: Rebuild headroom
steps.body: Keep enough free space to rebuild after losing a host: that is why slack is recommended.

courses.summary: How ESXi picks paths: PSA, NMP with SATP/PSP, HPP for NVMe, Round Robin tuning, and fixing a single-path performance bottleneck.
outcomes: Learners can explain PSA, NMP, SATP, PSP and HPP

scenes.text: A FC LUN has 4 paths, yet monitoring shows all I/O on one HBA.
Path selection policies decide.

steps.title: Layers
steps.body:
- **PSA**: framework for multipathing plugins.
- **NMP** (Native Multipathing Plugin) with **SATP** (array-type handling: e.g. VMW_SATP_ALUA, VMW_SATP_DEFAULT_AA) and **PSP** (path choice).
- **HPP** (High-Performance Plugin): default for local NVMe and NVMe-oF.
- Third-party MPPs from array vendors also exist.

steps.title: PSPs
steps.body:
- **VMW_PSP_MRU**: most recently used; stays on a path until it fails.
- **VMW_PSP_FIXED**: preferred path, returns to it when restored.
- **VMW_PSP_RR**: round robin across active (optimised) paths; vendors often recommend switching paths every **1 I/O** (iops=1).

steps.title: Runtime name
steps.body: `vmhba2:C0:T1:L4` = adapter vmhba2, channel 0, target 1, LUN 4. The NAA ID (naa.…) is the stable device identity.

Confirm SQL latency with DBAs
Update the storage onboarding checklist

closure.model: Root cause: LUNs from the new array defaulted to VMW_PSP_MRU (no claim rule), so all I/O used one path on vmhba2, causing kernel queueing (KAVG 31 ms). Fix: set RR iops=1 on devices and added SATP claim rule on all hosts. Verification: both HBAs active, KAVG <1 ms, DBA confirms normal query times.
